1	# Project Architecture — Guidebook
2	
3	This file describes how the Guidebook project is structured, where things belong, and how the layers interact. It governs and frames. It does not log specific issues, decisions, or session activity — that content lives in `decisions/`, `audits/`, `sessions/`, and git history.
4	
5	---
6	
7	<identity>
8	**Project:** Accessible Built Environments Guidebook — a reference document on architecture, accessibility, and built environment standards.
9	**Surface:** claude.ai chat with Code Interpreter.
10	**Repository convention:** single primary author; main branch protected by CI; data layer is authoritative.
11	</identity>
12	
13	<layer_model>
14	Three runtime layers govern Claude's behavior. Outer wins by default; layers override only with explicit named clauses.
15	
16	| Layer | Source | Scope |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| User preferences | `userPreferences-v*.md` | Cross-project |
19	| Project instructions (PI) | `governance/project-instructions-v*.md` | This project only |
20	| Skills + hooks + CI | `skills/`, `.github/workflows/`, `scripts/audit/` | Execution mechanics |
21	
22	PI overrides preferences only via explicit clause naming the rule and scope. Skills override PI on mechanics; PI governs whether a skill runs and under what conditions. Code-enforced checks (hooks, CI) trump text rules for the matching invariant.
23	
24	A cross-cutting **data layer** sits beneath all three: `data/guidebook.db` (canonical SQLite), schemas in `schemas/`, migrations in `scripts/migrations/`. The website and all derived artifacts read from this layer. Direct writes that bypass migrations are prohibited; CI enforces reproducibility.
25	</layer_model>
26	
27	<reference_files_pattern>
28	The PI declares which reference files it expects. Each file has a single defined purpose. Reference files contain **rules, taxonomies, and structured registries** — not session activity, dated reports, or transient state.
29	
30	Conventional locations:
31	
32	| Directory | Contents |
33	|---|---|
34	| `references/` | Production reference material consumed by ongoing work |
35	| `audits/` | Audit reports (dated); `audits/_archived/` for resolved findings |
36	| `decisions/` | Decision records (DR-YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md) and transient deployment queues |
37	| `sessions/` | Per-session records and `sessions/LATEST` pointer |
38	| `workplan/` | Active workplans; `workplan/_superseded/` for retired plans |
39	| `_archived/` | Files removed from active circulation but preserved for git history |
40	
41	When a reference file accumulates session-specific notes, dated commentary, or resolved-item logs, that content is extracted to the appropriate directory above. Reference files should read the same six months from now as they do today.
42	
43	**Decisions vs. Decision Records — two systems, different granularities.** `data/decisions/decision_register.yaml` (mirrored into the canonical `decisions` table) tracks granular in-session decisions with `D-NNNN` identifiers, schema-validated per `governance/decision-protocol.md` and checked by `scripts/decision_capture.py`. `decisions/DR-YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md` are standalone Decision Records, analogous to ADRs. The two are related but distinct, and **neither supersedes the other**: a DR typically records the reasoning behind one or more register decisions, and a register decision may exist with no DR at all. The naming is close enough that they have been mistaken for two representations of one dataset — they are not. *(Added 2026-08-15 per DR-2026-07-12-decision-tracking-naming-and-schema-doc-currency item 1, ratified 2026-07-13.)*
44	</reference_files_pattern>
45	
46	<skill_registry_pattern>
47	PI declares skill *assignments* — one-line entries naming which skills the PI itself invokes. Detail (location, status, purpose, triggers, dependencies) lives in `references/skill-registry.md`.
48	
49	Skill files are flat: `skills/<name>_SKILL.md`. Deprecated skills live in `skills/deprecated/` and are not loaded on trigger.
50	
51	**Universality requirement.** A skill file describes a protocol Claude executes when invoked. The protocol is generic over inputs: it cites no specific session IDs, no specific dates, no commit SHAs, no specific gaps, no embedded changelog. Project-specific state that the skill operates on lives in the database or in DRs the skill references by stable identifier. If a skill cannot be authored without specific project state, the state belongs in the PI rule that invokes the skill, not in the skill itself.
52	
53	**Placeholder convention.** When PI references a skill that does not yet have a file, the PI states "skill placeholder" or "no skill file exists" inline so the absence is intentional rather than a bug.
54	
55	**Drift between PI references and `skills/` content** is reconciled in `references/skill-registry.md`, not in PI itself.
56	</skill_registry_pattern>
57	
58	<enforcement_spectrum>
59	Rules live at one of five enforcement levels. Higher levels are more reliable but more expensive to author and maintain.
60	
61	| Level | Mechanism | Where | Reliability |
62	|---|---|---|---|
63	| 1 | Text rule | PI standing rules, DRs, skill descriptions | Low |
64	| 2 | Audit script | `scripts/audit/*.py` (CLI, manual or scheduled) | Medium |
65	| 3 | CI workflow, non-blocking | `.github/workflows/*.yml` with `continue-on-error: true` | High |
66	| 4 | CI workflow, blocking | `.github/workflows/*.yml` with `continue-on-error: false` | Highest |
67	| 5 | Pre-commit hook (local) | `.git/hooks/` | Highest (local) |
68	
69	**Promotion path.** New rules start at level 1 in PI standing rules. If the rule is mechanically checkable AND drift is observably costly, promote to level 2 by writing an audit script. If the rule must never drift in `main`, promote to level 4 by adding the audit script as a blocking job in CI. Pre-commit hooks (level 5) are deferred until contributor count exceeds one.
70	
71	**Demotion path.** Audit scripts that haven't found an issue in 6 months may be downgraded to scheduled execution (e.g., weekly cron via GitHub Actions) rather than per-push, to reduce CI cost.
72	
73	**Audit script style.** Module docstring lists checks numerically with rule provenance. Single `audit()` function with each check as a numbered SQL query or comparison. Reports formatted with `=` separators. Exit code 0 = pass, 1 = any issues found. Repository root resolved relative to `__file__` (no hardcoded absolute paths). DB path defaults to `data/guidebook.db` relative to repo root, overridable via `GUIDEBOOK_DB_PATH` environment variable to mirror `scripts/migrate_db.py`.
74	</enforcement_spectrum>
75	
76	<data_layer_pattern>
77	The SQLite database at `data/guidebook.db` is the single source of truth for project content. Markdown files and JSON exports may derive from it but never compete with it.
78	
79	**Schema discipline.**
80	- Schema changes ship as numbered SQL migrations: `scripts/migrations/NNN_<slug>.sql`. Forward-only. Tracked via `PRAGMA user_version`.
81	- Data changes ship as timestamped SQL migrations: `scripts/migrations/data_<YYYYMMDDHHMMSS>_<slug>.sql`. Forward-only, append-only. Tracked via the `data_migrations` table.
82	- The runner is `scripts/migrate_db.py`. It applies pending migrations on push and supports `--rebuild` for CI reproducibility verification.
83	
84	**Reproducibility invariant.** The committed `data/guidebook.db` must be reproducible from its migration history. CI rebuilds a fresh DB by replaying all migrations and compares key invariants against the committed file. Any direct DB write that bypasses the migration framework fails this check.
85	
86	**Schema documentation.** Pydantic schemas in `schemas/` mirror the SQLite layout. Drift between Pydantic and SQLite is a CI-detectable bug.
87	
88	**FK integrity.** `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` at session start; `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` returns empty on a healthy DB. Migrations that bulk-load may toggle FK enforcement off within their script body and back on at exit, but must leave the DB in a referentially-consistent state.
89	</data_layer_pattern>
90	
91	<bootstrap_pattern>
92	Each session loads project context via a bootstrap block at the start of the PI. The bootstrap pulls files from GitHub, queries `data/guidebook.db` for current state, and prints a status summary.
93	
94	**Constraints.**
95	- Halt on critical fetch failure; log `[GAP: <filename> — not present]` on non-critical failure.
96	- Total runtime budget: under 30 seconds. Total line count: under 100 lines.
97	- Use `gh` CLI when available; fall back to `curl` with PAT.
98	
99	When bootstrap grows past these budgets, extract the heaviest portion (typically SQLite state queries) to a `bootstrap-status` skill and leave a thin caller in PI.
100	
101	**Bootstrap-exempt operations.** Pure governance work on PI / preferences / architecture themselves; tooling questions not touching repo state; workflow conversations that do not touch repo content.
102	</bootstrap_pattern>
103	
104	<conflict_resolution>
105	| # | Situation | Resolution |
106	|---|---|---|
107	| 1 | Preference says X, PI silent | Preference applies |
108	| 2 | PI explicitly overrides a preference with named clause | PI applies |
109	| 3 | PI rule and skill content conflict on procedure | Skill wins on mechanics; PI wins on whether the skill runs |
110	| 4 | Text rule and CI workflow disagree on the same check | CI wins; record drift as `[ASSUMPTION]` in the next session record |
111	| 5 | Audit script (level 2) and CI workflow (level 4) check the same thing | CI is authoritative; the level-2 script remains for local debugging |
112	| 6 | Two skills overlap on the same trigger | `[GAP]` in `skill-registry.md` — disambiguate explicitly |
113	| 7 | Architecture spec and PI conflict | Architecture wins on architectural rules (layer ownership, enforcement spectrum, where things belong); PI wins on project specifics (skill assignments, terminology, identity) |
114	| 8 | Bootstrap procedure exceeds 100 lines or 30s runtime | Refactor: extract SQLite/state-query block to a `bootstrap-status` skill, leave thin caller in PI |
115	| 9 | A PI-referenced skill file doesn't exist | If labeled "placeholder" → OK (future hook); otherwise `[GAP]` — author the skill or remove the reference |
116	</conflict_resolution>
117	
118	<migration_and_growth>
119	**Adding a feature to PI.** Classify: preference-level (covered by user preferences, don't restate) · project-specific (add to PI) · procedural (extract to skill) · architectural (add here). Decide enforcement level. If level 2+, write the audit script as part of the change. If the change is workplan-level (affects multiple BPCs or rewrites a phase), write a DR in `decisions/` and reference it from the PI.
120	
121	**PI growth.** PI standing rules describe rules, not state. State content — "current AUTHOR-TITLE-ONLY counts," retraction banners, session-specific commentary — belongs in DRs, audit scripts, or the DB. When PI exceeds its size budget, audit for state content that should move out. The budget is set in the PI itself, not here.
122	
123	**Bootstrap growth.** When bootstrap exceeds its budgets in `<bootstrap_pattern>`, extract to a skill.
124	
125	**Shipping a new audit script.** Place at `scripts/audit/<name>.py` following the style in `<enforcement_spectrum>`. Reference from the corresponding PI standing rule. If blocking-in-CI, add a job to the appropriate workflow.
126	
127	**Adopting a new DR.** File at `decisions/DR-YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md`. If the DR sharpens or adds a standing rule, draft the corresponding PI bump in `governance/project-instructions-v<next>.md` and queue via `decisions/PI-update-needed.md`. The PI bump goes live only when the owner manually pastes the new content into claude.ai project settings — this layer is not API-writable.
128	
129	**Creating an `architecture/*.md` document that describes schema content.** It carries a currency header from creation: `**Governs schema work:** YES` or `**Governs schema work:** NO — historical record; see scripts/migrations/ for the current schema`. `scripts/migrations/` plus `PRAGMA user_version` are the authoritative schema source (`<data_layer_pattern>`); a prose description of the schema is normative only where it says so. Without the header, a reader cannot tell whether a dated design document still governs, and a generator or a future session may treat stale description as current — the phantom-table pattern. *(Added 2026-08-15 per DR-2026-07-12-decision-tracking-naming-and-schema-doc-currency item 2, ratified 2026-07-13.)*
130	
131	**Retiring content.** Move to `_archived/` rather than delete. Preserves git history while reducing namespace noise. Subdirectories under `_archived/` mirror the origin location.
132	
133	**Removing or renaming structural elements.** When any structural element is removed or renamed — XML tag, section heading, file path, identifier, schema column, skill name, table name — the change is not complete until a caller-sweep is performed. The verification pass searches non-archived locations for the old name and confirms zero orphan references remain. Renames substitute the new name in every caller. Removals decide per caller whether to delete the citation, redirect to a replacement section, or rewrite the surrounding context. Cleanup operations frequently introduce downstream broken references that pass naive verification — the change itself landed cleanly, but a caller two directories away still cites the old name. The check is not "did the removal succeed" but "are all callers now valid."
134	</migration_and_growth>
135	
136	<scope_assumptions>
137	The architecture currently assumes a single primary author, single deployment surface (claude.ai chat), and no concurrent contributors. Pre-commit hooks (level 5 enforcement), multi-surface PI specialization, and contributor-coordination mechanics are out of scope until those assumptions change.
138	</scope_assumptions>

557:RULE: Work from axes — no armchair umbrellas. All population/profile curation, demand-mapping, and specification proceeds FROM the functional axes (Layer 1 of the two-layer taxonomy, `governance/functional-taxonomy.md`) — the specific, architect-actionable, diagnosis-neutral, co-occurrence-native demand dimensions — never FROM broad population/profile umbrellas. The profile layer (Layer 2) is populated only with specific self-identified communities named on their own terms (co-produced; "nothing about us without us"); it is never a place to coin lumped coalition codes from an armchair. Broad umbrellas ("physically disabled"; clinical-cluster relabels like "energy-limiting chronic illness") are forbidden as profile codes: they collapse opposed and orthogonal design demands and erase specific communities — the pre-taxonomy category-thinking that §1.3, the irreducibility principle (functional-taxonomy §0.5), and mapping-confidence (§3.2) exist to end. A population is a mapping-confidence-weighted vector over axes, not a bucket. Umbrellas may exist only as additive cross-cutting tags over specifics, never as replacement codes. Provenance: three self-caught erasures in session 2026-07-21/22 — OFS→"ELCI" erased POTS (orthostatic/autonomic) + ME (exertional) + MCAS (chemical/immune), three distinct axis signatures; respiratory/pulmonary dismissed as "decomposed" (dyspnea ≠ fatigue ≠ chemical); "physically disabled/wheelchair users" erased the ambulatory and part-time-wheelchair disabled and buried the orthogonal upper-limb/reach axis. In each case the axis layer already held the distinctions the umbrella destroyed. Paired decision: DR-2026-07-22-work-from-axes.
559:ACTION: (1) Work from axes, not umbrellas. (2) If you catch yourself coining a population umbrella, STOP and decompose to axes. (3) Add profiles only as specific self-identified communities, co-produced — defer to community self-definition. (4) Use umbrellas only as additive cross-cutting tags, never replacement codes.
563:RULE: Design-equivalence exception to the anti-umbrella rule (amends 2026-07-22 "work from axes"; does NOT repeal it). An umbrella population code IS permitted when its members do not meaningfully differ *for design* — i.e., they converge on a shared/overlapping axis (access-need) signature — even where their medical etiology differs. Etiology is a clinical fact, not a design input; grouping on shared design demand erases nothing the guidebook acts on. The anti-umbrella rule protects DESIGN differences; it does not require splitting communities whose design demands are the same. An umbrella remains FORBIDDEN only when it erases design differences: collapsing opposed or orthogonal demands, or dropping distinct axis signatures (the OFS→"ELCI" case remains the paradigm forbidden umbrella — it dropped POTS/ME/MCAS's distinct signatures). Ratified exceptions (owner, 2026-07-23): **COM** (people with complex conditions — dysautonomia / long-COVID / MCAS / ME/CFS / POTS; high comorbidity; near-100% design overlap) and **BRAIN** (people with acquired brain injury — stroke / TBI / post-concussion). Permitted-umbrella test — all three required: (a) high within-umbrella comorbidity OR a near-identical design profile; (b) the UNION of member axis signatures is preserved on the umbrella code, never deduped away (verified at ratification: COM carries AX-CHM+AX-STA+AX-BAL+AX-THR+AX-COG-O; BRAIN carries AX-COG-O+AX-BAL+AX-AMB+AX-ARO+AX-COM-E+AX-SPR+AX-STA); (c) no opposed demand between members. This does NOT license coining further umbrellas that fail (a)-(c). Paired decision: DR-2026-07-23-population-schema-replace, which supersedes DR-2026-07-22-work-from-axes IN PART (this exception only; the base rule stands for all other cases).
